Fuse and Circuit Breaker. Safety devices that interrupt current flow when it exceeds a rated threshold, protecting circuit components and wiring from overcurrent damage, overheating, and fire. Fuses are single-use, while circuit breakers are reusable mechanical switches that automatically trip and reset.

A fuse is a resistive element, typically a metal alloy, that melts and opens the circuit when current exceeds its rating for a specified time—for example, a one ampere slow-blow fuse. Slow-blow fuses tolerate inrush current and prevent nuisance trips, while fast-blow fuses respond instantly to overcurrent and are used to protect expensive integrated circuits from shorts.

Circuit breakers use either a bimetallic strip that heats and bends open, or an electromagnetic coil that trips instantly during large currents. A lever flips to reset the breaker after it trips.

The I-squared-t rating, measured in ampere-squared times time, defines fuse energy. Higher values tolerate longer overloads before opening, which is important in circuits with startup surges. A thermal trip current is typically one-point-five to two times the continuous rating. A magnetic trip triggers at ten to twenty times the rating or higher, with a millisecond response.

Ground-fault circuit interrupters detect imbalance between supply and return current—leakage to ground—and trip in roughly twenty-five milliseconds. This is critical for safety in wet environments.

The fuse and breaker rating must match the wire gauge. Undersizing the rating risks nuisance trips, while oversizing allows the wires to overheat and fail, creating a fire hazard. When multiple protection devices are placed in series, they are designed so the upstream device clears faults before downstream devices fail—this is called coordination.
